verified_claim: NCI explains that chronic exposure to carcinogens in cigarette smoke produces genetic damage involved in multistep lung carcinogenesis. The article specifically identifies the association between cigarette smoking and DNA adduct formation in human lung tissue as evidence of tobacco-related genetic damage.
limitation_note: DNA adduct formation demonstrates chemical injury to DNA but does not establish that every lesion becomes a persistent mutation. Some lesions may be repaired or eliminated. The article supports chronic smoking-related lung tissue DNA injury without specifying an exposure threshold or proving that every exposed individual develops measurable injury or cancer.

provisional_claim: Candidate: accumulated tobacco-related genetic damage in lung tissue contributes to multistep lung carcinogenesis, rather than guaranteeing cancer.
verified_passage_locator: NCI Lung Cancer Prevention Health Professional Version → The Biology of Carcinogenesis; Risk Factors → Factors Associated With Increased Risk of Lung Cancer → Cigarette smoking; paragraph on genetic damage driving multistep carcinogenesis
verified_claim: NCI describes lung epithelial carcinogenesis as a multistep process involving initiation, promotion and progression. The article explains that genetic damage from chronic exposure to tobacco carcinogens contributes to this process and identifies DNA adduct formation in human lung tissue as evidence of tobacco-related genetic injury. This supports lung-cell DNA injury as a contributory mechanism increasing the likelihood of lung cancer development.
limitation_note: The source does not establish that an individual DNA adduct or DNA lesion independently predicts or inevitably causes lung cancer. DNA damage may be repaired or eliminated and cancer development generally requires the accumulation and selection of relevant oncogenic alterations. The evidence supports a contributory risk mechanism within tobacco-related carcinogenesis, not an isolated quantitative risk estimate for DNA damage or a deterministic transition to malignancy.
review_note: Reviewed NCI Lung Cancer Prevention Health Professional Version, particularly The Biology of Carcinogenesis and Risk Factors → Cigarette smoking. The source explicitly places chronic tobacco-related genetic injury within multistep lung carcinogenesis. This supports DNA damage in lung cells → Increased risk of lung cancer development as RISK_FACTOR_FOR, conditional on the accumulation of relevant alterations and other carcinogenic processes. DNA injury alone is not sufficient to establish cancer. AI-assisted review; human confirmation pending.
